questions.question: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS vs Pulsar — how do you pick a messaging system?
questions.title: Messaging Systems: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS vs Pulsar
questions.direct_answer: Four dominant messaging systems, each optimized differently: **Kafka** is a distributed commit log — pull-based, high throughput, durable event streaming, replay; best for events, analytics pipelines, CDC. **RabbitMQ** is a traditional broker — push-based (with prefetch), flexible routing (exchanges), great for task queues and RPC; weaker for high throughput. **SQS** is fully managed AWS — zero ops, at-least-once, no ordering (standard) or FIFO queues, great for task queues on AWS. **Pulsar** combines Kafka-style streaming with RabbitMQ-style queuing, has tiered storage and multi-tenancy. Rule of thumb: Kafka for events at scale, RabbitMQ for flexible routing + RPC, SQS for AWS-native task queues, Pulsar if you need both streaming and queuing in one system.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of messaging system trade-offs, not just surface features
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to Kafka for everything (overkill for simple task queues); defaulting to RabbitMQ (doesn't scale to event streaming); ignoring managed options
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss pull vs push, commit log vs queue, consumer groups vs competing consumers, message ordering guarantees, backpressure, durability, operational complexity, and cost models

sections.title: Four Systems, Four Philosophies
sections.content:
Messaging systems are not interchangeable. Picking the wrong one causes architectural pain: scaling walls, unexpected ordering bugs, operational burden, or cost overruns.

**Kafka — distributed commit log** LinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 as a durable event log.
- It's not a traditional queue — it's an append-only log partitioned across brokers, retaining messages for a configurable period (7 days default).
- Consumers track their own offset and pull messages.
- Multiple consumer groups read the same data independently.
- Optimized for high-throughput event streaming (millions of msg/sec per broker), exactly-once semantics within Kafka, and replay (read historical data).

**RabbitMQ — traditional message broker** A classic AMQP broker with exchanges, queues, and bindings.
- Push-based (broker pushes to consumers, with prefetch limit).
- Flexible routing: direct, topic, fanout, headers.
- Excellent for task queues (competing consumers) and RPC patterns.
- Weaker for high-throughput streaming — tens of thousands of msg/sec per node, not millions.

**SQS — AWS managed queue** Fully managed, zero ops, pay per message.
- Two types: **Standard** (at-least-once, no ordering, massive throughput) and **FIFO** (exactly-once, per-group ordering, 3000 msg/sec per group).
- Simple API: SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage.
- No routing logic — producers write, consumers read.
- Best on AWS where managed-ness wins over feature richness.

**Pulsar — unified streaming + queuing** Yahoo open-sourced Pulsar.
- Architecturally splits compute (brokers) from storage (BookKeeper) — independent scaling.
- Supports both streaming (like Kafka) and queuing (like RabbitMQ) with different subscription types.
- Tiered storage: hot data on disk, cold data in S3. Multi-tenancy with quotas.
- Steeper learning curve, smaller community, but technically compelling.

**Other notable options:** NATS (ultra-low latency pub/sub), Redis Streams (simple, good for small scale), ActiveMQ (older, still used in enterprises), Kinesis (AWS managed Kafka-like), Google Pub/Sub.

sections.title: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Dimension | Kafka | RabbitMQ | SQS | Pulsar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Model** | Distributed log (pull) | Broker + queues (push) | Managed queue (pull) | Broker + BookKeeper (pull) |
| **Throughput** | Very high (1M+ msg/s/broker) | Moderate (50K msg/s/node) | Very high (Standard) / 3K/s (FIFO) | Very high |
| **Latency** | Low (~10ms) | Very low (1–5ms) | Medium (10–50ms, long polling) | Low (~10ms) |
| **Durability** | Replicated log, disk | Persistent queue option | Replicated by AWS | BookKeeper replicas |
| **Ordering** | Per partition | Per queue | None (Standard) / per group (FIFO) | Per partition |
| **Retention** | Time or size-based (days/weeks) | Until consumed + ack | 14 days max | Configurable + tiered to S3 |
| **Replay** | Yes (seek to offset) | No | No | Yes |
| **Routing** | Topic only | Rich (direct, topic, fanout, headers) | Basic | Topic + subscriptions |
| **Delivery guarantees** | At-least-once, exactly-once (within) | At-least-once | At-least-once | At-least-once, exactly-once |
| **Consumer model** | Consumer group (partition assignment) | Competing consumers (push) | Competing consumers (pull) | Exclusive, shared, key-shared, failover |
| **Operational complexity** | High (Zookeeper/KRaft, partitions) | Medium (broker, cluster) | Zero (managed) | Very high (broker + BK) |
| **Cost model** | Hardware + ops | Hardware + ops | Per message + data | Hardware + ops (self-host) |
| **Best for** | Event streaming, analytics, CDC | Task queues, RPC, flexible routing | AWS task queues, zero ops | Multi-tenant, hybrid streaming/queuing |

sections.title: Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Pick Kafka when:**
- Event-driven architecture with high message volume (> 100K msg/sec)
- Need replay (consumer reprocessing historical events)
- Multiple consumer groups read same stream (pub/sub with durability)
- CDC (change data capture): Debezium streams DB changes to Kafka
- Log aggregation or analytics pipelines
- Ecosystem: Kafka Connect, Schema Registry, Kafka Streams

**Pick RabbitMQ when:**
- Task queues with flexible routing (topic exchanges, fanout)
- RPC patterns (reply-to queues)
- Lower throughput but flexibility matters more
- Short-lived messages (no need for replay)
- Polyglot: AMQP clients in every language
- Team familiar with traditional broker model

**Pick SQS when:**
- On AWS, want zero ops
- Task queue model fits (one message, one consumer processes and deletes)
- Cost per message is acceptable ($0.40 per million)
- Simple API is enough (no complex routing)
- Lambda triggers: SQS natively triggers Lambda

**Pick Pulsar when:**
- Need both streaming and queuing in one system
- Multi-tenant SaaS: Pulsar's namespaces/tenants/quotas are first-class
- Extreme retention: tiered storage to S3 for cheap long-term
- Geo-replication requirements (Pulsar has better native geo-replication)

**The hybrid reality**

Many orgs run multiple:
- Kafka for event streaming, CDC, analytics
- SQS for AWS-native background tasks
- RabbitMQ for legacy RPC or team familiarity
- NATS for ultra-low-latency internal messaging

**Cost considerations**

*Kafka*
- Self-hosted: $0 licensing, high operational cost (3+ brokers, Zookeeper/KRaft, monitoring)
- Confluent Cloud: $$$ at scale but simpler
- AWS MSK: managed but still pay per broker-hour

*RabbitMQ*
- Self-hosted: $0 licensing, lower ops than Kafka
- AWS MQ: managed RabbitMQ; expensive per instance
- CloudAMQP: managed SaaS

*SQS*
- Pay per request: $0.40 per million for Standard, $0.50 for FIFO
- No broker to manage
- Cheap for low/medium volume; expensive at very high volume (billions/day)

*Pulsar*
- Self-hosted: complex; 3+ brokers + 3+ BookKeeper nodes
- StreamNative: managed SaaS

**Start with simpler, evolve as needed**
- Small team, low volume, AWS: SQS
- Need flexible routing, moderate volume: RabbitMQ
- Event streaming becomes strategic: Kafka
- Need multi-tenancy or very long retention: consider Pulsar

sections.title: Nuanced Trade-offs
sections.content:
**Pull vs push delivery.** - **Kafka/Pulsar/SQS (pull)**: consumer requests messages.
- Natural backpressure (slow consumer = slow pull rate).
- Requires consumer to poll.
- **RabbitMQ (push)**: broker pushes to consumer with prefetch limit.
- Lower latency, but can overwhelm slow consumers if prefetch is too high.

**Consumer groups vs competing consumers.** - **Kafka consumer group**: each partition assigned to one consumer in the group.
- Parallelism limited by partition count; ordering preserved per partition.
- **RabbitMQ competing consumers**: all consumers pull from same queue; any can get any message.
- Ordering not preserved across consumers.
- **Pulsar key-shared**: like Kafka — same key goes to same consumer. Pulsar shared: like RabbitMQ.

**Ordering guarantees.** - **Kafka**: per-partition total order. Cross-partition: no guarantee.
- Key messages by entity (order_id) for related events together.
- **RabbitMQ**: per-queue FIFO if single consumer; order breaks with competing consumers.
- **SQS Standard**: no ordering.
- SQS FIFO: per message-group-id ordering.
- **Pulsar**: per-partition ordering; key-shared subscription preserves order per key.

**Retention and replay.** - **Kafka**: retention time/size based; replay by seeking to offset.
- Critical for analytics and reprocessing.
- **RabbitMQ**: message deleted after ack.
- Stream plugin in newer versions adds replay but not as first-class.
- **SQS**: max 14 days retention; no replay.
- **Pulsar**: tiered storage retains for months cheaply.

**Exactly-once claims.**
- **Kafka**: transactional producer + idempotent consumer = exactly-once within Kafka. Doesn't extend to external DBs.
- **RabbitMQ**: at-least-once; manual dedupe on consumer.
- **SQS FIFO**: deduplication window of 5 minutes via deduplication ID.
- **Pulsar**: similar to Kafka.

**Operational complexity.**
- **Kafka**: high. Zookeeper (pre-3.x) or KRaft (new). Partition rebalancing, broker failures, consumer lag monitoring.
- **RabbitMQ**: medium. Cluster management, queue mirroring.
- **SQS**: zero (managed).
- **Pulsar**: very high. Brokers + BookKeeper + Zookeeper.

**Message size.**
- **Kafka**: 1MB default (configurable up to 10MB); not ideal for large payloads. Use references (S3 URL in message).
- **RabbitMQ**: 128MB default but impacts memory.
- **SQS**: 256KB max; use S3 pointer for larger.
- **Pulsar**: 5MB default.

**Schema management.**
- **Kafka + Confluent Schema Registry**: centralized schema evolution (Avro/Protobuf/JSON). Compatibility rules enforced.
- **RabbitMQ**: no native schema; app-level.
- **SQS**: no native schema.
- **Pulsar**: native schema registry.

**Geo-replication.**
- **Kafka MirrorMaker 2 / Confluent Replicator**: async cross-region replication.
- **RabbitMQ Shovel / Federation**: basic.
- **SQS**: single-region; use SNS cross-region if needed.
- **Pulsar**: native geo-replication, best-in-class.

**Monitoring needs.**
- Kafka: consumer lag is the key metric; also broker ISR, partition skew.
- RabbitMQ: queue depth, consumer count, unacked messages.
- SQS: ApproximateNumberOfMessages, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage.
- Pulsar: subscription backlog, broker load.

**Security.**
- All four: SSL/TLS, SASL/ACLs.
- SQS: IAM policies integrate with AWS identity.
- Kafka: OAuth (Confluent), mTLS, Kerberos.

**Kinesis is AWS-managed Kafka-like.** Similar pull-based log model; cheaper than running your own Kafka on AWS. Fewer features than Kafka (no Schema Registry natively, shards vs partitions). Good if you're AWS-first and don't need full Kafka feature set.

**Google Pub/Sub.** Similar to SQS but with pub/sub fan-out. Lambda-equivalent integration.

**The default recommendations in 2026:**
- **On AWS, simple task queues**: SQS
- **Event-driven at scale**: Kafka
- **Flexible routing, RPC, task queues (lower volume)**: RabbitMQ
- **Multi-tenant SaaS, long retention**: Pulsar
- **Ultra-low latency pub/sub**: NATS

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four dominant systems**, each optimized differently — no one-size-fits-all
- **Kafka** = distributed commit log; pull-based; high throughput; retention and replay; best for event streaming at scale
- **RabbitMQ** = traditional broker; push-based with prefetch; rich routing; best for task queues and RPC at moderate scale
- **SQS** = fully managed AWS queue; zero ops; best for AWS-native task queues; cheap at low/medium volume
- **Pulsar** = split storage + compute; streaming + queuing in one; multi-tenant; best for complex platforms with long retention
- **Pull vs push** — pull gives natural backpressure; push lowers latency but risks overwhelming consumers
- **Ordering per partition/queue**, not cross-partition; key messages by entity for related events
- **Exactly-once is local** — Kafka's exactly-once is within Kafka; external DB writes need idempotent consumers
- **Cost models differ** — Kafka: hardware + ops; SQS: per message; managed Kafka: expensive but simpler
- **Monitor consumer lag** (Kafka), queue depth (RabbitMQ), message age (SQS) as primary health signals

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Four dominant messaging systems, each with a different architectural philosophy. Picking wrong causes scaling walls, unexpected ordering bugs, operational burden, or cost overruns.

**Kafka — distributed commit log**
- Append-only log partitioned across brokers
- Pull-based: consumers track their own offset
- Retention for days or weeks
- Multiple consumer groups read the same data independently
- Very high throughput: millions per second per broker
- Best for event streaming, analytics pipelines, change data capture
- Operational complexity: Zookeeper or KRaft, partition management, consumer lag monitoring

**RabbitMQ — traditional broker**
- Exchanges, queues, bindings; rich routing (direct, topic, fanout, headers)
- Push-based with prefetch limit
- Excellent for task queues and RPC patterns
- Tens of thousands per second per node; not millions like Kafka
- Messages deleted after consumer ack
- Best for flexible routing and lower-volume workloads

**SQS — AWS managed queue**
- Zero ops; fully managed
- Standard queue: at-least-once, no ordering, massive throughput
- FIFO queue: exactly-once, per-group ordering, 3000 per second per group
- Simple API: SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage
- Cost per message: $0.40 per million Standard, $0.50 FIFO
- Best for AWS-native task queues; cheap at low and medium volume

**Pulsar — unified streaming + queuing**
- Stateless brokers plus BookKeeper for storage; independent scaling
- Supports both streaming (Kafka-like) and queuing (RabbitMQ-like) via subscription types
- Tiered storage: cold data to S3 cheaply
- Multi-tenancy first-class
- Best for platforms needing both models and long retention

**Key architectural differences**

*Pull vs push*
- Kafka, SQS, Pulsar are pull: natural backpressure, consumer controls rate
- RabbitMQ is push with prefetch: lower latency but slow consumers can be overwhelmed if prefetch too high

*Consumer model*
- Kafka consumer group: each partition assigned to one consumer; parallelism limited by partitions; ordering per partition
- RabbitMQ competing consumers: all pull from queue; ordering lost across consumers
- SQS: similar to competing consumers
- Pulsar: exclusive, shared, key-shared, failover subscriptions

*Ordering*
- Kafka: per-partition total order; cross-partition no guarantee
- RabbitMQ: per-queue FIFO with single consumer; breaks with competing
- SQS Standard: no ordering; FIFO: per message-group-id
- Pulsar: per-partition

*Retention and replay*
- Kafka: time or size based retention; replay by seeking to offset
- RabbitMQ: deleted after ack; stream plugin adds limited replay
- SQS: max 14 days; no replay
- Pulsar: tiered storage for months cheaply

**Decision framework**

*Pick Kafka when*
- Event-driven architecture, 100K+ messages per second
- Need replay for reprocessing
- Multiple consumer groups on same stream
- Change data capture with Debezium
- Ecosystem: Kafka Connect, Schema Registry, Kafka Streams

*Pick RabbitMQ when*
- Task queues with flexible routing
- RPC patterns with reply-to
- Polyglot: AMQP clients everywhere
- Lower throughput but flexibility matters more

*Pick SQS when*
- On AWS, want zero ops
- Task queue model fits
- Lambda triggers natively
- Cost per message acceptable

*Pick Pulsar when*
- Both streaming and queuing in one system
- Multi-tenant SaaS
- Extreme retention with tiered storage
- Geo-replication requirements

**Exactly-once reality**
- Kafka's exactly-once is within Kafka only; doesn't extend to external DB writes
- SQS FIFO has 5-minute dedupe window via deduplication ID
- Pulsar similar to Kafka
- Always combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers for true effectively-once

**Cost models**
- Kafka: $0 license, high ops cost; Confluent Cloud expensive at scale
- RabbitMQ: $0 license, lower ops; CloudAMQP or AWS MQ managed
- SQS: pay per request; cheap low/medium, expensive at billions
- Pulsar: complex to self-host; StreamNative managed SaaS

**The hybrid reality**
- Most orgs run multiple systems
- Kafka for event streaming and CDC
- SQS for AWS-native background tasks
- RabbitMQ for legacy RPC
- NATS for ultra-low-latency internal

**The strategic answer**
- No one-size-fits-all; pick based on throughput, retention, routing, ops budget
- Start simple; evolve
- On AWS, small team: SQS
- Event streaming strategic: Kafka
- Flexible routing: RabbitMQ
- Multi-tenant or very long retention: Pulsar

questions.question: What's the difference between a message broker, a message bus, and an event bus?
questions.title: Message Broker vs Message Bus vs Event Bus
questions.direct_answer: A **message broker** is a separate infrastructure component (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Kafka) that sits between services and routes/persists messages — it's a network-hop and is the default for cross-process messaging. A **message bus** is an *in-process* publish-subscribe abstraction (Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher`, Guava `EventBus`, .NET MediatR) — handlers are JVM objects, no network involved, and a crash loses unhandled events. An **event bus** is usually a synonym for message bus but used in the context of event-driven (rather than command/RPC) communication; the same in-process tools serve both roles. The choice is really 'cross-process broker' vs 'in-process bus' — the broker/bus terminology only adds confusion when used loosely.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can clearly distinguish in-process pub/sub from cross-process messaging infrastructure and pick the right tool for a use case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` as a substitute for Kafka — it's in-process only, has no durability, and crashes lose unhandled events
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss when an in-process bus is genuinely the right choice (decoupling within a service, transactional event listeners, modular monoliths) and when promoting to a broker is necessary (cross-service, durability, replay)

sections.title: The Real Distinction Is 'In-Process' vs 'Across the Network'
sections.content:
The terminology in this space is loose enough that the same words mean different things in different communities. The useful, concrete distinction is **scope and durability**, not naming:

**Message broker (cross-process, durable, infrastructure).** A separate piece of infrastructure — RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Kafka, Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub — that producers connect to over the network.
- The broker persists messages, routes them via queues/topics/exchanges, and delivers them to consumers in other processes (often other machines).
- If a consumer is down when a message is published, the broker holds the message until the consumer comes back.
- This is the default for any messaging that crosses a service boundary.

**Message bus / event bus (in-process, in-memory, library).** An in-JVM publish-subscribe mechanism.
- The publisher and subscribers are objects in the same process, often the same Spring `ApplicationContext`.
- There is no network hop, no separate infrastructure to deploy, and no persistence — if the JVM crashes between publish and handler invocation, the event is gone.
- Examples: Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` + `@EventListener`, Google Guava `EventBus`, .NET `MediatR`, the typical 'domain events' pattern in DDD.

**Event bus** is typically just a message bus used in an event-driven style (publish-subscribe with multiple unrelated consumers reacting to events) rather than a command style (one publisher addresses one specific handler). Some authors reserve 'message bus' for command-style and 'event bus' for event-style, but most practitioners use them interchangeably.

The trap is treating the in-process bus as a drop-in for a broker. Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` is excellent for decoupling components within a service — but it's not a substitute for Kafka. If two different services need to react to an event, you need a broker; an in-process bus can't reach across processes by definition.

sections.title: Broker vs In-Process Bus — Concrete Differences
sections.content:
| Aspect | Message Broker | In-Process Bus |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Cross-process, cross-machine | Single JVM only |
| **Examples** | RabbitMQ, Kafka, ActiveMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub | Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher`, Guava `EventBus`, MediatR |
| **Transport** | Network (TCP, AMQP, Kafka protocol) | In-memory method invocation |
| **Persistence** | Yes — survives broker restart and consumer downtime | No — events lost on JVM crash |
| **Delivery guarantees** | At-least-once / exactly-once configurable | Best-effort; default Spring is synchronous (in caller thread) |
| **Async by default** | Yes | No (Spring `@EventListener` is sync; need `@Async` to switch) |
| **Operational cost** | Separate cluster to deploy, monitor, secure, back up | Zero — it's a library |
| **Latency** | ~1-10 ms typical | Microseconds |
| **Throughput** | Millions of msgs/sec (Kafka), 50K+ (RabbitMQ) | Limited by JVM CPU only |
| **Replay** | Yes (Kafka log retention) | No |
| **Schema evolution** | Schema Registry, version negotiation | Java type contract — pure compile-time |
| **Multi-language** | Yes — any client that speaks the protocol | JVM-only |
| **Right for** | Microservices, async work queues, event sourcing fan-out | Decoupling within a service, modular monoliths, transactional domain events |

sections.title: Same Use Case, Two Implementations
When Each Belongs in a Real System
sections.content:
**Use an in-process bus when:**
- The publisher and all subscribers live in the same Spring application — modular monolith, single-bounded-context service.
- You want to decouple cross-cutting concerns (audit logging, metrics, cache invalidation) from the core flow without introducing distributed-systems complexity.
- You need handlers to participate in the same database transaction (`@TransactionalEventListener` with `BEFORE_COMMIT` / `AFTER_COMMIT` phases).
- A future migration to a broker is acceptable — the publish API is similar enough that swapping `ApplicationEventPublisher` for `KafkaTemplate` is a refactor, not a redesign.

**Promote to a broker when:**
- Subscribers live in a different service (or could in the future).
- Events must survive publisher restarts and consumer outages — durability is the single biggest reason to use a broker.
- You need replay — a new subscriber that wants to process all historical events can't do that against an in-process bus.
- Multiple consumer instances must split the work (Kafka consumer groups / RabbitMQ competing consumers).
- Throughput exceeds what synchronous in-process listeners can absorb.

**Hybrid is normal.** The same service often uses both. `ApplicationEventPublisher` fires for in-process side effects (metrics, cache invalidation, transactional projection updates), and `KafkaTemplate` fires the same logical event over the wire for other services. The Outbox pattern formalizes this: write to the database and the outbox in one transaction, an `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` triggers the local in-process side effects, and a separate poller or Debezium publishes the outbox to Kafka for cross-service delivery.

**Anti-pattern to avoid: 'event-bus monolith on Kafka'.** Putting every internal cross-method call through Kafka because 'events are good' produces extreme operational complexity, multi-millisecond latency between objects that used to call each other directly, and observability nightmares. Kafka is for inter-service integration; in-service decoupling belongs on the in-process bus.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Broker vs bus is really cross-process vs in-process.** Brokers are infrastructure; buses are libraries.
- **Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` is in-process only** — synchronous by default, lost on crash, no replay.
- **Brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) provide durability, network reach, and multi-language clients** at the cost of operating a separate cluster.
- **`@TransactionalEventListener` is the killer feature of the in-process bus** — handlers can run before or after commit, transactionally tied to the publishing transaction.
- **The Outbox pattern combines both** — in-process listeners for local side effects, broker fan-out for cross-service delivery, with the outbox table guaranteeing durability.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The terminology is loose but the practical distinction is clear.
- A message broker is cross-process infrastructure — Kafka, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, SQS — that sits between services and persists messages.
- A message bus or event bus is an in-process publish-subscribe library — Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher`, Guava `EventBus`, MediatR in .NET — where publisher and subscribers are objects in the same JVM.

**Brokers:**
- Network hop, persistent, survive consumer downtime
- Configurable delivery guarantees (at-least-once, exactly-once)
- Required for any messaging that crosses a service boundary
- Cost: a separate cluster to deploy, monitor, and secure

**In-process buses:**
- Method invocation, no network, no persistence
- Lost on JVM crash unless you use the outbox pattern alongside
- Default in Spring is synchronous in the caller thread; switch to `@Async` for true async
- Excellent for decoupling within a service — metrics, audit, cache invalidation
- Killer feature: `@TransactionalEventListener` lets handlers run before or after the publisher's transaction commits, transactionally bound to it

**Event bus vs message bus:**
- Practically synonyms; some authors reserve 'event bus' for event-driven (publish/subscribe with unrelated consumers) and 'message bus' for command-style (one publisher addresses one handler)
- The same in-process tools serve both roles

**When to choose each:**
- In-process bus when the publisher and all subscribers live in the same Spring application — modular monoliths, single-service decoupling
- Broker when subscribers live in another service, when events must survive crashes, when you need replay, or when throughput exceeds what in-process listeners can absorb
- Hybrid is the norm: the in-process bus fires local side effects, and the same logical event goes out to Kafka via the Outbox pattern for cross-service delivery

**Anti-pattern:**
- Putting every internal method call through Kafka because 'events are good' — extreme operational cost, multi-ms latency between objects, observability nightmares
- Kafka is for inter-service integration; in-service decoupling belongs on the in-process bus

My default for a new Spring service is `ApplicationEventPublisher` plus `@TransactionalEventListener` for local concerns and the Outbox pattern fanning out to Kafka for cross-service consumers — that gives you both worlds without the anti-patterns of either extreme.

speakable_v2.hook: The terms get used loosely. The real split is cross-process vs in-process — and that one decision drives durability, network cost, and replay.

groups.heading: Message broker
groups.text: Infra between services. Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS. Producers send over the network. The broker keeps the message and re-delivers when the consumer wakes up.

groups.heading: Message bus / event bus
groups.text: An in-JVM pub-sub library. Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher, Guava EventBus. One process, no network, no persistence. The two names mean the same thing.

values: a cluster to run and watch

beats.text: Reach for a broker when subscribers live in another service. Reach for an in-process bus to decouple cross-cutting work inside one Spring app. The gotcha most candidates miss: ApplicationEventPublisher fires sync in the caller thread, so a JVM crash before the listener runs drops the event on the floor.

paragraphs: events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(...)) inside @Transactional fires the in-process event. A @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) handler picks it up.
kafka.send('orders', orderPlaced) ships the same event to consumer services. The outbox keeps DB write and broker write in sync.

speakable_v2.cap: Broker for cross-service durability and replay. In-process bus for in-app decoupling. Outbox bridges them when both matter.
